snippet.title: The Man Who Sold the Eiffel Tower Twice - and Faked $2.3M
snippet.description:
Victor Lustig sold the Eiffel Tower — twice — and flooded America with $2.3 million in counterfeit cash, the most audacious confidence scheme of the 20th century. He never owned the tower. No one did. In the spring of 1925 he forged the letterhead of the French Ministry of Posts, summoned six scrap-metal dealers to a suite at the Hôtel de Crillon, and told them the rusting monument was to be quietly demolished and sold off. One dealer, André Poisson, handed over 1.2 million francs — plus a bribe on top — and was too ashamed to ever call the police. Lustig worked ocean liners with a mahogany box he swore printed money. He talked Al Capone out of $50,000 and left the mob boss grateful. He never carried a gun, never broke a lock. His only weapon was a handshake, and the willingness of strangers to believe him.

This is the true story of the smoothest con man who ever lived — how a peasant boy from Bohemia invented a count, sold a monument he did not own, disarmed the most dangerous man in America, and became the counterfeiter the U.S. Treasury could not stop.

snippet.title: How Nazis Built a Secret Counterfeit Factory to Cripple Britain’s Economy
snippet.description:
During World War II, Nazi Germany launched one of the most ambitious financial warfare operations ever attempted. Hidden inside a concentration camp, a secret team of prisoners was forced to produce nearly perfect counterfeit British banknotes in a scheme designed to undermine Britain's economy and fund Nazi intelligence operations.

Known as Operation Bernhard, this extraordinary project became the largest counterfeiting operation in history. The forged currency was so convincing that even experts struggled to distinguish it from genuine Bank of England notes.

In this documentary, we uncover the shocking story behind Hitler's secret counterfeit factory, the prisoners who created millions in fake money, and the plan that nearly turned the British pound into a weapon of war.

What you'll discover:
• The origins of Operation Bernhard
• How the Nazis recreated British banknotes
• The concentration camp prisoners behind the operation
• The role of counterfeit money in Nazi espionage
• The hidden treasure dumped in Austrian lakes
• Why this remains the greatest counterfeiting scheme ever attempted

This is a story of deception, survival, espionage, and one of the strangest battles fought during World War II.

snippet.title: How One of the Biggest Counterfeiter's in History Rose to Power
snippet.description:
#shorts 

On June 19, 1911, a new government presided over portugal. They had taken over from the monarchy which preceded them, and they hoped that moving toward a system of elected leaders would solve so many of the problems that plagued the nation. Instead, this would be one of the most unstable times in the counties history, filled with attempted and successful coups, persecution of the religious, and constant conflict. But in this time, a man saw opportunity for those who were willing to do what others couldn’t, blocked by morals or ability, but he would be the exception. As political turmoil was enveloping the country the economy was quick to follow stuck in a continuous decline, leaving its gold reserves as the lowest in Europe. The Bank of Portugal, which was partly a government entity and partly in private ownership issued far more notes than were permitted causing it’s currency to plummet in relation to the pound sterling. 
And it was during this devastating period in the nation’s history that one of the largest scams ever to be perpetrated would occur. And there’s likely no other point in Portugal’s history that could have happened. The Bank Note Scandal would end up consisting of 1-5% of the entire country’s GDP. As Lord Macmillan of Aberfeldy put it, “it was “a crime for which, in the ingenuity and audacity of its conception, it would be difficult to find a parallel.” This nearly perfect crime as well as the subsequent attempted takeover of the Central Bank of Portugal was the product of one man Artur Virgilio Alves Reis and the way he committed and was caught was simply incredible.

snippet.title: How Counterfeit Money Actually Works | How Crime Works | Insider
snippet.description:
Jeff Turner counterfeited over $1 million in US currency. He forged the 1996-series $100 bill and later the 2013 "blue note." He was indicted on federal conspiracy charges in 2019 and cooperated with the Secret Service, eventually serving 10 months in prison. According to Turner, the Secret Service said the bills he was manufacturing were the highest quality they'd seen in over 25 years. 

Turner speaks to Insider about the materials and processes required to make fake money. He talks through how to spot a fake bank note. He also discusses cartel forgeries from Colombia and Peru, and the "supernotes" the US has accused North Korea of making. Nowadays, Turner works as a printer in Knoxville, Tennessee. He speaks about spotting fakes and frauds on his YouTube channel.

snippet.description:
Discover the captivating story of Frank Bourassa, one of the most prolific counterfeiters in US history, who forged an astonishing $250 million in US bank notes. This documentary delves deep into how Frank, initially a brake factory owner in Trois-Rivieres, Quebec, Canada, turned to counterfeiting after facing burnout in his legitimate business.

Frank Bourassa's journey into the world of fake money began with a simple desire to stop working himself to death and ultimately led to him running a sophisticated counterfeit operation. Using advanced printing techniques, Frank produced millions of high-quality forged bank notes, complete with security features like watermarks, which even included images of former US president Andrew Jackson.

Despite his efforts to distribute the counterfeit money across continents, Frank's scheme was eventually thwarted when the Secret Service caught up with him, leading to a raid where $1 million in fake cash was found. His arrest shocked the counterfeit industry and highlighted the intricate security features of US currency.

Frank Bourassa's story doesn't end with his arrest; after spending just six weeks in prison, he struck a plea deal by disclosing the location of another $200 million in unused counterfeit money, drastically reducing his potential prison time. Today, Frank has returned to legal ventures, using his knowledge to help others avoid counterfeiting.

This video explores every angle of Frank Bourassa's life as a counterfeiter, from the initial motivation through his arrest and beyond, examining the legal consequences and the impact on the counterfeit industry. snippet.title: "FLAWLESS" — World's biggest, best counterfeiters busted 💷
snippet.description:
Mobsters are always hustling to make a buck. Sometimes that is taken quite literally. The Mob Reporter here with news of a huge Mafia-linked underground mint — that produced a river of fake money that flooded Europe and a police bust this month that took down the largest euro banknote counterfeiting ring in history.
NEW: JOIN ME ON PATREON: https://www.patreon.com/TheMobReporter
The euro is the official currency of most members of the European Union. It is second only to the U.S. dollar in terms of most used and most traded currency in the foreign exchange market. Their values are fairly comparable. 
Things started to unravel by accident in 2017 after a kidnapping in the Italian city of Benevento, 50 kilometres northeast of Naples, home of the Camorra, one of Italy’s powerful Mafia organizations. When a local nicknamed “Nero” was arrested for the kidnapping, police found he was carrying counterfeit euros. 
When anti-counterfeiting specialists examined the notes, they were astounded. They were the best they had ever seen. The fake money was almost flawless. One cop said it was the work of “true artists.” The bills proved to be high quality fakes that required high-level technical expertise, modern offset printing machines and quality raw materials. They looked and felt like the real deal. The counterfeiters had mimicked all the main security features of genuine euro banknotes. Police said they couldn’t tell the difference with the naked eye. Even older money detectors were fooled. 
When the same quality counterfeit €50 notes started popping up elsewhere, police started chasing down the source. In February 2018, a 70-year-old typographer who ran a print shop was arrested. Buried on his property, police found nine plastic barrels stuffed with the fake bills with a face value of €41 million. Police also found the metal plates needed for the offset printing along with test printing sheets.
The tentacles of an experienced criminal network with distribution channels nationally and abroad started to be uncovered. A raid five months later found an illegal minting workshop that was punching out 50-euro cent coins in Lombardy. Investigators kept working.
One by one, couriers were picked off over months, caught carrying bundles of the counterfeit cash destined for foreign markets. The counterfeit bills were filtered into the economy in two ways: a network of friends made small purchases with the change from the store coming back in real currency; on a larger scale, the notes were sold in bulk at a steep discount over face value, apparently €8 for a fake €50 euro note.
And on July 15, 2020, police sprang simultaneous raids in Italy, France and Belgium, codenamed Operation Nero — named after the poor sap who triggered the probe when he was caught with fake notes. In all, 44 people were arrested and assets worth €8-million were frozen or seized. Three clandestine printing facilities were uncovered. The ring is believed to have produced and distributed more than three million counterfeit banknotes for a total face value of over €233 million. That’s more than US$271 million. European police officials estimate this counterfeiting ring produced 25% of all counterfeit euro banknotes in circulation. 
The alleged masterminds behind the organization were a 69-year-old man from Benevento known as “The Baron” and a 66-year-old from Naples known as “the Counterfeiting King.”
The Camorra mafia was linked in to move it around Italy and across Europe. Adding a touch of tabloid glamour, one of the alleged bulk couriers was the grandson of famous French actress Catherine Deneuve. I loved her in The Hunger. Her grandson was arrested in France and faces extradition to Italy. A wiretap allegedly caught him admiringly describing the counterfeit notes “magnificent.”
I suspect their handiwork will be floating around Europe and around the world for years to come.

Government agents soon visited the magazine, demanding they hand over the artwork. Despite this legal scare, MAD continued to print novelty currency.
